source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: First LLM paper to frame red herrings as an Einstellung/fixation test. Quiz-show walls have 16 clues, 4 hidden groups, and deliberate decoy groups. No model solved the task; GPT-4 was best but far below an expert human baseline.
numbers: Dataset: 62 train, 62 validation, 494 test walls. GPT-4 10-shot solved 6 of 494 walls (239 correct groups); GPT-3.5-turbo 10-shot solved 0 (140 groups). Static embeddings (GloVe, FastText) solved 0 walls.
quote: creative problem solving ... fixation effect and Einstellung paradigm
limits: Fan-site human data; about 10% of clues out of vocabulary for embeddings; only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tested well (LLaMA could not follow instructions); no chain-of-thought run.
agent_relevance: Decoys that fit a second group are a cheap, scoreable Einstellung probe for our agent. Use the wall format to test guardrail G1 and S3 history.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall) - red-herring ablation
finding: Removing red herrings raised GPT performance sharply. This is the causal evidence that the decoys, not clue difficulty, hurt the models.
numbers: 10-shot solved walls out of 494: GPT-4 6 (original) vs 59 (OCW-Randomized, groups swapped across walls) vs 471 (OCW-WordNet, no decoys). GPT-3.5: 0 vs 10 vs 415. Correct groups GPT-4: 239 vs 595 vs 1926.
limits: Synthetic variants also change difficulty and domain (WordNet relations are easier); the paper reports no significance test.
agent_relevance: Template for an A/B test: same items with and without a lure. Report the lure-minus-no-lure gap, not only accuracy.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall) - connection naming and in-context examples
finding: More in-context examples did not fix fixation. On naming the connection, best GPT-4 10-shot F1 was far below humans.
numbers: Human: about 80% of connections correct. GPT-4 10-shot: 41-45% F1 (ROUGE/BERTScore). Exact match under 15%. Clues echoed inside predicted connections in 8.2% of cases. GPT-4 grouping scores moved little from 0-shot to 10-shot (e.g. WD 58.2 to 56.6).
limits: Chain of thought and tree of thoughts explicitly left for future work, so no scaffold result exists here.
agent_relevance: Plain few-shot demonstrations do not buy flexibility. Do not expect a bigger example set to loosen a lure.

source: Sergeyuk et al. (2023) Overcoming the Mental Set Effect in Programming Problem Solving
finding: Luchins-style Einstellung test with developers: many fell back on a habitual indirect Python idiom instead of the recommended direct one. A colour change and a 'forget earlier solutions' cue did not reliably help.
numbers: 129 surveyed; 57 showed at least one mental set; 39 finished. About 44% of the sample showed the set. Set holders had less Python experience (T(126.998)=2.806, p=.006). Participants said they rethought in 54% of cases yet rated interventions unhelpful (M=0.97, SD=1.18 on 0-5).
limits: Small final N; code-style habits, not bugs; human developers, not LLMs; null results with 3 groups are low powered.
agent_relevance: A verbal 'forget the previous solution' instruction is weak even in people. Our reframe step should change the problem, not only tell the model to ignore prior work.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: First direct Luchins-style order test on LLMs, adapted from DeCaro (2016) mathematical equivalence problems. Shortcut-first versus complex-first orders were compared on three models.
numbers: 6 complex plus 6 shortcut problems; each condition has only 6 items. Few-shot exact match (SP, SP+CPF, CP, CP+SPF): Llama-3.1-8B 0.16/0/0/0; Llama-3.1-70B 0/0.16/0/0.66; GPT-4o 0.33/0.66/0.66/0.83.
limits: Workshop-scale: 6 items per cell, no significance tests, no repeats, one prompt style. Order effect is not cleanly separated from in-context-example effect. Reported as 'investigative'.
agent_relevance: Shows the order paradigm can be run on LLMs in minutes, but needs far more items and seeds before it can bind a design decision.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set? - effect of chain of thought
finding: Adding zero-shot chain of thought raised accuracy but made the solutions longer: shortcut problems that need one step took three steps. The authors read this as a mental set induced by CoT.
numbers: Few-shot+CoT exact match (SP, SP+CPF, CP, CP+SPF): Llama-8B 0.5/0.66/0.33/0.83; Llama-70B 0.5/0.66/0.66/0.83; GPT-4o 0.66/0.66/0.83/0.83. Steps = 3 in every cell. Humans need 1 step on shortcut items.
limits: Step count may reflect the CoT format, not a set. 6 items per cell.
agent_relevance: Forced stepwise reasoning can lock in the long procedure. Supports G1: do not apply a fixed multi-step routine by default.

source: Haq et al. (2025) - paradigm design (DeCaro 2016)
finding: Design is reusable: number pairs are identical across complex and shortcut sets, so only strategy differs. Order of presentation (complex first or shortcut first) is the manipulation.
numbers: Problems such as 7+5+9=7+? (shortcut: cancel repeated addend) versus 7+5+9=3+? (complex). Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o.
limits: Arithmetic equivalence is a narrow domain and easy for frontier models today.
agent_relevance: Cheap probe with a known right answer and a countable efficiency measure (steps).

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: Medical abstraction-and-reasoning set built to trigger Einstellung: a familiar pattern is the wrong answer. Most LLMs did worse than physicians.
numbers: 100 questions written to resist memorisation; 53% include an option to seek more information. Physicians (5): 66% (SE 5.3). Most LLMs under 50%; some near or below 20%. Gemini-1.5-Pro 50%, o1 48%.
quote: LLMs ... perform poorly compared to physicians on M-ARC
limits: Only 100 items and 5 physicians; chain-of-thought prompting followed MMLU-Pro code; no scaffold ablation; models are early 2025.
agent_relevance: Item style to copy: the habitual answer looks fluent and wrong, and the right action is often 'get more information'.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC) - calibration
finding: Models were overconfident on the very items they failed. Larger models were better calibrated but still overconfident. o1 repeated the usual 'recheck the blood pressure' move where common sense said act.
numbers: Top models (o1, Gemini-pro, Claude-opus, Llama-3.1-70B) show overconfidence at low accuracy. Smaller models (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-flash, Claude-Sonnet) were more overconfident at lower accuracy.
limits: Verbalised-confidence and probability measures differ across vendors; no numeric ECE quoted in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Model confidence cannot be the trigger for doubt in a fixation case. This matches the schema rule that impasse signals come from code, not self-report.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving
finding: Re-ran M-ARC on newer reasoning models. Strong reasoning models now match physicians; weaker or non-reasoning ones do not. This is the main counter-result to 'LLMs are inflexible'.
numbers: Best: Claude 4.1 Opus mean 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763) over 15 runs. Physician mean 0.66 (CI 0.55-0.75). No significant difference for Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning vs humans (paired bootstrap). Highest reasoning effort used.
limits: Same 100 items as Kim 2025, now public and possibly contaminated; 5 physicians; vendor reasoning settings differ.
agent_relevance: Test-time reasoning effort is a candidate lever against Einstellung. Compare our scaffold against a plain high-effort run.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving - human-miss subset
finding: On the 20 items most physicians got wrong, the best model was confidently right more often than humans. Suggests models can be less prone to a human-style set on some items.
numbers: Human-miss set: 20 of 100 items; human accuracy 36% (CI 26-46%) there vs 73% on the rest. Claude-4.1-Opus: decisively correct on 55.0% (Wilson 90% CI 39.9-80.0), decisively wrong 25.0%, indeterminate 20.0%. Abstract: top 5 models 55-70% correct with high confidence.
limits: n=20 items; selecting items by human failure inflates the contrast (regression to the mean). Models and humans fail for different reasons.
agent_relevance: Model fixation and human fixation are different sets of items. Do not assume human Einstellung items catch the model.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving - sample consistency for deferral
finding: Entropy-based and agreement-based sample consistency over 15 runs stayed informative on the adversarial set, and newer reasoning models gave better Brier scores.
numbers: 15 stochastic runs per model; Wilson 90% interval used to label each item confidently correct, confidently wrong or indeterminate.
limits: No single headline AUROC in the text I read; authors note a distribution shift versus MMLU-Pro.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run disagreement is a usable code-side impasse signal (G1), better than asking the model if it is sure. Agreement is still only a hint (G4).

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs
finding: Counterfactual benchmark: each case has a control and a minimally edited 'trap' where one discriminating fact flips the diagnosis. Einstellung is scored as getting the control right but answering the control label on the trap.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs. Bias Trap Rate = P(trap answered with the control/bias label | control correct). Cases filtered by an LLM judge committee, threshold 0.5.
quote: relying on statistical shortcuts rather than patient-specific evidence
limits: Synthetic cases made by an LLM pipeline from a symptom-disease knowledge base; trap difficulty not human-validated at scale in what I read.
agent_relevance: Best paired design found so far: same item with and without a lure, plus a conditional rate. Reuse for our A/B test.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs - results by model
finding: Frontier models had high baseline accuracy but high trap rates; accuracy and robustness did not move together. Authors claim scale does not cure it.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-pro Bias Trap Rate 60.90%. Text: GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-pro have top baseline accuracy and trap rates above 50%. No correlation between model size and robustness. Qwen3-32B: baseline 40.25, robust 11.86, trap rate 43.46.
limits: Table 1 columns were scrambled in my text extraction, so per-model values other than those quoted are not reliable. Conflicts with Shidara 2026 (reasoning models improved); tasks and metrics differ.
agent_relevance: Strong priors can raise lure-following. Test scaffold gains per item type, not on average accuracy.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs - failure modes
finding: Error analysis of GPT-5 on trap cases splits failure into not noticing the key fact, shallow reasoning, and talking itself into the prior.
numbers: GPT-5: blindness (key evidence ignored) in over 35% of error cases. Where the evidence was noticed: 43% underthinking, 22% overthinking (motivated reasoning toward the prior).
limits: Labels assigned by LLM judge; one model; percentages as quoted in the paper text.
agent_relevance: Three distinct fixes are needed: force evidence extraction, force a check of the alternative, stop rationalising. Maps to S3 history and the reframe operator.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs - ECR-Agent and agent baselines
finding: Scaffold built against Einstellung: causal-graph reasoning plus an evidence audit (DCI), and a critic-driven memory of validated reasoning paths (CGME). Both parts helped. Multi-agent debate frameworks did not.
numbers: Qwen3-32B base: acc 40.25 / robust 11.86 / trap 43.46. +DCI: 55.49 / 19.94 / 38.32. +DCI+CGME: 69.49 / 24.21 / 33.75. MDAgent and DyLAN (same base) showed low robust accuracy (about 8-10% per text) and high trap rates; authors blame consensus bias.
limits: Single base model; benchmark and method from the same authors; code not yet released; trap rate still 33.75% after the scaffold.
agent_relevance: Closest published scaffold test for this subfield. Gains came from structured evidence checks, not from more voters: agrees with G4 (no voter diversity fix).

source: Gu and Shi (2025) Einstellung Rigidity Index in continual learning
finding: Borrows the word Einstellung for neural nets: old features block learning a new task. Defines three numbers: Adaptation Delay, Performance Deficit and relative Shortcut Reliance. On their test the rigidity did not appear.
numbers: CIFAR-100, ResNet-18, 8 superclasses in phase 1, magenta patch shortcut in phase 2, threshold 0.6; methods SGD, online EWC, DER++, GPM, DGR. Continual learners reached threshold earlier (negative AD) and the patch acted as a distractor (negative SFRrel). DGR was the exception (PD 0.107 +/- 0.039; often never crossed the threshold in 50 epochs).
limits: One benchmark, one backbone; text reports both 'slightly lower final accuracy' and negative PD, so sign reporting is inconsistent. Weight-space rigidity, not reasoning rigidity.
agent_relevance: Useful idea only: measure speed to threshold with and without the cue (masking). Not evidence about LLM agents.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: When the model must decide by itself whether to revise, accuracy falls. With an oracle label it rises. This is the machine version of 'a rethink prompt does not escape the set'.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 (rounds 1-2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: 2023-era models; does not test reasoning models; prompts were generic 'review your answer'.
agent_relevance: Backs G1 and G2: revise only from real failing output, not from an opinion. A reframe prompt without a signal can hurt.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Over 200,000 simulated conversations. Models make an assumption early, propose a final answer too soon, and then lean on it. Once off track they do not recover. This is a fixation on a first commitment.
numbers: Average drop 39% from single-turn to multi-turn across six generation tasks. Aptitude (best-case) loss about 15%; unreliability up 112%.
limits: Not an Einstellung test by design; the prior commitment here is the model's own early guess, not a taught routine.
agent_relevance: Do not let the first attempt stay in context unchecked. Supports restating the problem from scratch (reframe) on a signal.

source: Tang (2026) Generalization or Memorization? Brittleness Testing for Chess-Trained Language Models (KinGPT)
finding: Chess puzzle scores of chess-tuned LLMs are mostly pattern-matching: a 25M model trained only on (position, best move) beats larger chess LLMs. A verifier in the loop helps a general LLM a lot.
numbers: KinGPT 25M exceeds 3B ChessGPT on a 600-puzzle mate-in-N suite and 4B C1-4B on a 20-theme benchmark. LLM-Modulo on RedPajama-3B: best-move accuracy 1.2% to 21.2%; move validity 19.3% to 95.3%.
limits: Beginner-level puzzles; shows pattern reliance, not an Einstellung (better-solution) test as in Bilalic. Brittleness shown by perturbation.
agent_relevance: Chess LLMs are strong pattern users, so the Bilalic trap (familiar solution hides a better one) is a natural next test. An external checker beats more training.

source: Meszaros, Reizinger and Huszar (2025) Out-of-distribution tests reveal compositionality in chess transformers
finding: A 270M chess transformer keeps choosing legal moves and good moves on out-of-distribution puzzles, but loses to explicit search on Chess960 variants.
numbers: 270M-parameter transformer; tested on OOD positions, puzzles and Chess960; the gap to symbolic search is smaller against humans on Lichess.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; no Einstellung-specific measure.
agent_relevance: Learned pattern policies adapt partly; explicit search covers what pattern recall misses. Fits an operator that branches a search when pattern recall disagrees with a check.

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix: Evaluation Framework for Creative Defixation Prompting in LLMs
finding: Tests human defixation methods (SCAMPER, TRIZ, C-K, brainstorming, design thinking, two AI-specific prompts) on five LLMs. All 25 method-based prompts beat the control on novelty, but outputs stay homogenised across models.
numbers: Models: Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o, Grok-4.1-fast-reasoning; 3 runs each. Gains of best alternatives per metric are roughly +10% to +41% (figure labels partly garbled). Llama and Grok most novel; differences significant by t-test.
quote: prompting models remain constrained in a fixation space
limits: Measures idea novelty, not correct-answer fixation; distance metrics depend on embeddings; vendor temperatures differ.
agent_relevance: Short, plain prompts ('wild, bold, surprising') worked as well as long method prompts. Defixation prompts shift output but do not remove the shared attractor.

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix - fixation on task wording
finding: Task attributes steer fixation: negative keywords partly reduce it; surprising keywords raise novelty at the cost of diversity. Models produced more ideas of lower novelty on common tasks.
numbers: All reported keyword and brief-type differences statistically significant (their Tables 3-5).
limits: Design-brief ideation; no ground truth correctness.
agent_relevance: Wording of the problem statement is itself an anchor. Reframing needs a different representation, not a different tone.

source: Liu, Karimnazarov and White (2025) Trapped by Expectations: Functional Fixedness in LLM-Enabled Chat Search
finding: Human study of functional fixedness in using an LLM: prior habits with search engines or voice assistants shape prompts, and unmet expectations push adaptation.
numbers: 450 crowd participants, six decision tasks, multi-prompt ChatGPT conversation. Virtual-assistant users wrote directive command prompts.
limits: Abstract page only. Fixedness is in the human user, not the model.
agent_relevance: Shows the same set effect on the human side of our loop. Our interface should not teach users a single prompt habit.

source: Leins et al. (2026) LLM orchestration methods across chess puzzles, competitive programming and math
finding: Self-Refine, Best-of-N and Debate, each tuned with GEPA, gave only moderate gains and cost much more. Gains did not grow with difficulty.
numbers: Largest average gain 4.6 points over optimised CoT, 4.5 over task-only. Token use 2-4 times task-only. Strong method-by-backbone interactions in all three benchmarks. Five backbones.
limits: Abstract page only; per-method numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Generic re-asking loops do not buy flexibility. Backs the schema choice of code-gated, signal-driven operators over always-on debate.

source: Sergeyuk et al. (2023) background: forgetting and task-irrelevant change in the lab
finding: Related-work section cites human results that a 'forget the earlier solutions' cue (Storm and Angello 2010; Tempel and Frings 2019) and task-irrelevant context change (Vallee-Tourangeau et al. 2011; Tukhtieva) weaken Einstellung in the lab.
numbers: No new numbers; secondary citation only.
limits: Cited, not re-read at source. The programming study found neither helped in code.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: cues that work on abstract lab problems may not transfer to a rich domain.

source: Lovett and Anderson (1996) History of success and current context in problem solving (ACT-R)
finding: Older computational account: an ACT-R model picks strategies by their record of past success, which reproduces set effects in a building-sticks task and explains why a successful old strategy blocks a better one.
numbers: Not opened this session; figures not recorded.
limits: Details are from memory (Sergeyuk 2023 cites an ACT-R chapter only) and must be checked before use.
agent_relevance: A success-history score per strategy is a ready-made design for S3 history: track which approach worked and require a trigger before choosing it again.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones
finding: Founding chess study (human angle, covered by other agents). Experts who found a familiar solution kept looking at it while saying they sought better; cited by Kim 2025 as the model for the effect.
numbers: Not opened by this angle; see the human-angle files for the numbers.
limits: Cited in Kim 2025 (ref. 27) and Haq 2025 only.
agent_relevance: Chess analogue for a machine test: a position with a familiar long mate and a shorter hidden mate.
